- If sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.5) or negative (≤ -0.5) in recent days, model tends to over- or under-forecast; adjust forecast slope downward or upward accordingly.
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., >10% from prior day), model often overshoots and fails to correct — reduce forecast slope or add early mean-reversion term.
- When sentiment is mixed or neutral (0.0–0.25 or -0.25 to 0.0), model tends to drift toward historical mean — apply slight downward bias if recent price is above 30-day average.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below forecast), model is overconfident — reduce forecast magnitude by 5–10% for next period.
- For 30-day horizon, model often fails to capture short-term volatility — add sentiment-weighted volatility buffer (e.g., ±2–3% of recent 7-day range) to forecast bounds.
- If sentiment history includes multiple “1.0” or “-1.0” entries, model should be more conservative — cap forecast range within ±10% of recent 14-day average.
